Second team moves into the bio-bubble | New Scientist

# Second team moves into the bio-bubble

By Bernice Wuethrich

 19 March 1994 

 Undaunted by the problems that bedevilled their predecessors, a second batch of human guinea pigs entered Biosphere 2 last week. The team of six biosphereans will spend 10 months sealed inside the glass-and-steel structure in the Arizona desert. 

 The new team’s entry marks a change in emphasis for the project, says John Corliss, the research director. Now that the basic operational systems have been worked out, the project can focus on research that will transform the imitation world into a laboratory for global ecology, he says. 

 However, while some scientists agree that the project provides a unique opportunity to carry out innovative research, others suggest that the opportunities are being squandered by a short-sighted management. And there is still uncertainty about just how sustainable the artificial ecosystem is. 

 Although the first biosphereans emerged rather thinner than when they went in, they did succeed in growing about 85 per cent of the food they needed. But the five natural ecosystems established in Biosphere 2 have had more variable success. Shrubs and grasses are overrunning the desert area because the artificially generated climate is too moist for the desert plants. On the other hand, the rainforest has prospered, doubling in size. Job’s tears, a grass that normally grows about 60 centimetres tall in the tropics, has become a giant of around 4 metres, says Michael Balick, the director of economic botany at the New York Botanical Garden. 

 The artificial ocean also seems to be in trouble, says Robert Howarth, an oceanographer at Cornell University, New York. The plankton levels are incredibly low and corals are slowly starving. 

 Howarth believes the ecosystems could be sustainable if the owner of Biosphere 2, Space Biosphere Ventures, invested more money in the project. One of the most serious problems for the first group of biosphereans was the steady decline in the concentration of oxygen inside the structure. Because the soil in the glasshouse had been made too rich, the population of soil bacteria proliferated massively. The microbes consumed more oxygen than anyone had allowed for, leaving the human occupants short of breath. The easy – but costly – solution would have been to replace the 30 000 tonnes of soil. 

 Howarth and Wallace Broecker, the geochemist at the Lamont-Doherty Geological Observatory in New York who identified soil bacteria as the cause of the oxygen loss, urged Space Biosphere Ventures to postpone the next manned phase of the project until they had addressed the basic biogeochemical imbalance inside Biosphere 2. By failing to do so, the company is passing up important opportunities, says Howarth. 

 If a balance was established and the system could be reliably controlled, it would be possible to alter the amount of carbon dioxide to simulate conditions of global warming, then analyse how ecosystems respond. ‘I don’t think they understand Biosphere 2’s value,’ says Howarth. 

 A few scientists have made the most of the opportunities offered by Biosphere 2. John Avise, a geneticist at the University of Georgia in Athens, introduced two closely related species of mosquito fish to study how they evolved in places where their distribution overlapped. He found that there are extremely rapid genetic changes as the fish interbreed in the overlapping zones. ‘It gave us a new perspective on the dynamics of populations and how dramatically genetic change can take place,’ he says. ‘We did one nifty little thing with the fish, but there are lots of neat experiments you can envision. It is a unique setting.’ 

 Many researchers believe that some of the changes in the way the project is being run are positive. This time around, scientists will be allowed in, and samples and specimens will be allowed out. The researchers will enter through an airlock for stays of several days to several months. Their effect on the atmosphere should be quantifiable. Last time, no one was allowed in or out except during medical emergencies. This limited the amount of science that could be done, as the biosphereans were concerned almost entirely with ensuring their own survival.
